messages.body_plain:
Hi Aiden,

More than likely these misfitting items are due to choosing a less flexible IRT model and less to do with sparse response categories. If you choose something more flexible, which are potentially more representative of the probabilistic relationship with the latent trait, then you'll likely notice large improvements in the item-fit statistics. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Cursos,

The code looks okay to me, though I have not tested it. My only major comment would be to use the 'MAP' estimator for fscores() to obtain point estimates that are not influenced by numerical integration. Regarding your question, I'm not quite sure why you are looking for a table with 3 columns. The model you've fit is a latent growth curve model, so the first 2 latent traits saved from fscores() represent the latent intercept and linear slope parameters for each participant.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: calibration
messages.body_plain:
In basic, The Rasch model constrains the slope as 1 to solve item parameter indeterminacy issues. Therefore calibrated person parameter has not mu=0 even the mirt::mirt() uses the MMLE. Moreover, Under the MMLE, if you do not know any item/person parameters, set the prior distribution of the person parameter as \theta~N(0,1); excluding the Rasch model.

Best,
Seongho

messages.body_plain:
You need to specify the covariance parameter in the model (mirt assumes the factors are orthogonal by default). There is a COV argument in the mirt.model() syntax which does this. It sounds like for your repeated measures design you just need to fit two separate correlated models: a two-factor model for A-B, and a two-factor model for 1-2. So long as there are no cross-loadings then you'll obtain the same results, however you'll avoid having to evaluate 4-dimensional integrals (which starts to get inaccurate and slow).

Phil

This makes sense. There's theoretically 7^9 unique response patterns required to saturate the G2 statistic (each of which needs 3+ observations to be stable). So mirt doesn't compute this statistic when the data is too sparse.

> I also tried using the M2 function, but it tells me that it cannot be calculated since df is too low. I tried adding
>

>
> to the mirt function when I run it to obtain CFI and TLI, but those two indicators are also NaN.

Right, it looks like you're in the no-mans land for goodness of fit statistics. There is a fix for this via a hybrid approach for M2, but it requires a pretty big rewrite that I haven't found the time or inspiration to do yet.

Not so much no. Though given that you're using the graded response model you could get a decent proxy with the lavaan package and it's model-fit statistics. HTH.

library(mirt)
mod <- mirt(Science, 1)

fscores(mod, response.pattern = newdata)
